name: Head cone shaping

card.summary: The elongated, conical skull shape produced historically by binding an infant's head, and a related ancient Egyptian wax head-cone adornment, discussed as an alternative ideal of head shape.
card.note: Binding is an infant practice historically; reported complications include asymmetry, bleeding, infection and tissue damage.

quick.overview:
Head cone shaping refers to the elongated, conical skull seen in many ancient and traditional cultures, produced by binding or pressing an infant's head with boards or cloth while the skull is pliable. In those societies it signalled status or group identity and was valued for appearance.

The name is also confused with the 'head cone' of ancient Egypt, a wax cone shown on heads in tomb art, which was a worn ornament rather than a change to the skull. In looksmaxxing discussion the elongated-skull ideal is a historical and fringe topic; shaping the adult skull this way is not described in the sources.
quick.how: Historical cranial deformation applied bands or boards soon after birth, often for around two years. Because it depends on an infant's malleable skull, it is a cultural practice documented by anthropologists, not a routine available to adults. The Egyptian cones were beeswax shells set on top of the head or wig.
quick.risks: Reported complications of cranial deformation include facial and cranial asymmetry, bleeding, infection and tissue necrosis, though much of the effect partly fades after infancy as the body compensates. Studies of Peruvian skulls found no significant difference in cranial capacity.

lead: Head cone shaping is a term applied to two different things: artificial cranial deformation, the intentional reshaping of an infant's skull into an elongated or conical form, and the ancient Egyptian head cone, a conical adornment shown on heads in New Kingdom art. In appearance terms, the first is a reshaping of the skull itself and the second is a worn accessory that gives a pointed, elevated head profile.[1][2]

Cranial deformation predates writing. Hippocrates described the 'Macrocephali' around 400 BCE, and the practice appears among the Alans and Huns, the Maya, Inca and Tiwanaku peoples, groups in the Pacific such as Vanuatu, and the Mangbetu of Africa. Proposed motives include signalling status or group identity, aesthetic preference, and beliefs about intelligence or spiritual closeness.[1]
The practice is described only as a historical and cultural phenomenon in the sources cited here, with no modern guidance on shaping the skull.

angle.text: In societies that practised it, binding was used to give children an elongated head regarded as beautiful or a mark of status. It works only on infants whose skulls are still pliable.

paras: Devices were applied soon after birth, often for about two years, and produced flat, elongated, rounded or conical shapes. Researchers have not agreed a single classification; one scheme uses round, fronto-occipital and sagittal types.[1]

Regions include Iran, Central Asia and the Pontic steppe; the Maya, Inca and Tiwanaku in the Americas; the Philippines, Vanuatu and New Britain; the Mangbetu in Africa; and Tanegashima in Japan. The article says the practice still occurs in Vanuatu, while the Mangbetu custom began dying out in the 1950s.[1]

Head cones appear in New Kingdom tomb paintings and reliefs from about 1550 to 1070 BCE, worn by men and women at banquets and rituals. Two beeswax cones, each about 8 cm tall, were recovered from non-elite graves at Amarna, with no scent or fat residues found in chemical analysis; scholars link them to ritual and rebirth themes.[2]

Peruvian samples showed no significant difference in cranial capacity from unmodified skulls. The practice can cause facial and cranial asymmetry, bleeding, infection and tissue necrosis, and most effects fade after infancy as growth partly compensates.[1]
